title: My brother's keeper (Genesis 4:9–16)
hookLine: Cain asks "Am I my brother's keeper?" and the rest of the Torah answers him

cards: Cain comes back from the field alone. Two brothers went out; one walks home. And God asks a question God already knows the answer to, the way God asked Adam in the garden.
In the old JPS translation: "Where is Abel thy brother?" It's a door held open. Cain could say, I did something terrible.
Instead he shrugs. "I know not; am I my brother's keeper?" A lie, then a question thrown back in God's face.
The story, and the Torah after it, spend a long time answering it.

teach.b: The Hebrew for keeper is shomer: a guard, a watchman, someone who keeps a thing safe. Its root, shamar, to keep, is the same one the Torah uses for keeping Shabbat. So Cain's question is sharp: am I supposed to guard him?

teach.h: THE BLOOD CRIES FROM THE GROUND.
teach.b: God answers with a sound: "the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto Me from the ground." The rabbis noticed that the Hebrew word for blood there is plural. Bloods.
The Mishnah, in tractate Sanhedrin, explains: Abel's blood, and the blood of every child and grandchild who would have come from him. Cain didn't end one life.
He ended a world. A few lines later, the same Mishnah gives the teaching you met a week ago: whoever destroys a single life, it's as if they destroyed a whole world. Then the surprise.
Cain is punished: he'll be a wanderer, and the ground won't yield for him. He cries that it's too much to bear. And God puts a sign on him, so that no one who finds him will kill him.
Even the murderer is kept. God answers Cain's question by doing the very thing Cain refused to do. The rest of the Torah keeps answering.

teach.h: NEITHER SHALT THOU STAND IDLY BY.
teach.b: In Leviticus: "neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour." A few lines later: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." And the Talmud makes it a principle: all Israel are responsible for one another.
Am I my brother's keeper? The Torah, and the rabbis after it, keep answering: yes.

how: Jewish teaching draws on Cain's question and on Leviticus 19:16 to say that people are responsible for one another; the Talmud's principle that all Israel are responsible for one another is often cited when communities organize help for someone in trouble.

o: a mark of protection God gives someone
a stranger who wanders with no home
a guard, someone who keeps another safe

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: Abel and all who'd have come from him
so no one would kill him

s: God answers Cain's question with an argument
God answers with a sound: the voice of Abel's blood crying from the ground.
the Hebrew word for blood in God's answer is plural
"bloods": the Mishnah reads it as Abel and every descendant who would have come from him.
God leaves Cain unprotected after the murder
God puts a sign on Cain so that no one who finds him will kill him.

games.q: you're Cain. you've come back from the field alone, and God asks, "where is Abel thy brother?" what do you say?
o: "I know not; am I my brother's keeper?"
games.why: he lies, then throws a question back. and the Torah keeps answering it: yes.

practice: Bring to mind a sibling, or an old friend who has drifted a little, and see their face. Notice what you don't know: how they're sleeping, what's worrying them this month.
If you pray, hold them in your prayer; if you don't, hold them in your attention for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Shomer, Hebrew for a guard or keeper, from the root shamar, to keep. Cain's shrug, and the Torah's long answer: people are asked to guard one another.

orig.note: Hebrew: "am I my brother's keeper?" shomer, a guard, from shamar, to keep.

carryVoice: Your line: yes, you are. Tomorrow, a man called righteous in his generation. Day thirty-one, done.
